# Sets, Power Sets, & Cross Products

## Goals

- Use sets to describe groups of people, and ask who can be singled out.
- Count a union without double counting: **inclusion-exclusion**.
- Explore the Empty Set.
- Distinguish **element** ($\in$) vs **subset** ($\subseteq$).
- Define the **power set** $\mathcal{P}(S)$ and its **cardinality**.
- Define **Cartesian product** $A\times B$.

Say once: len(df[C]) and C.sum() are the same number. len counts the rows of
the set; C.sum() counts the Trues in the mask (True is 1) -- the indicator sum
|A| = sum of 1_A(x) on Sets = Filters on Rows. Later slides use .sum(); it's
what students will see in real pandas code, and it never builds the subset.
A hidden cell above this one loads the class into df when the page opens (no

# Who Are We?

## Set Design {.activity .smaller}

Get into groups of 4 with your cards.

::: {.write-space}
1. What is the fewest questions that give all 4 of you different answers? Which ones?
2. Find a question all 4 of you answer the same way.
3. What's special about **your** group? Write a rule $\{\, x : P(x) \,\}$ that includes all 4 of you and nobody else in the room.
:::

<style>.reveal .write-space li { margin-bottom: 3.5em !important; }</style>

::: notes
Each question is a set; two people are told apart when they are not in exactly
the same sets. One question splits a group into at most 2, so 4 people need at
least 2 questions (2^2 = 4 answer pairs). A group holding a twin pair (Amara &
Ravi, Leila & Hana, and others: 78 of the 100 share a card) can never be told
apart -- that is the next slide, for the whole class.
2. A shared answer puts the whole group inside one set: all in C, or all in
   C^c. Some groups share nothing -- also worth saying out loud.
3. Start from the shared answers (an AND); check who else in the room fits by
   asking them to stand. If no AND works, an OR of the four exact descriptions
   always does -- unless someone outside the group holds the same card as
   someone inside it. "Describe a group and nobody else" is a marketing
   segment, and it is the same question as the next slide.
Chose a set of columns all at once, not ask-then-branch: no decision trees
(DSCI 221).
:::

## Who Can Be Identified? {.smaller}

Six yes/no questions give $2^6 = 64$ possible cards.

* We have $100$ students and only $64$ possible cards. What does that guarantee?
* In real data, a few "questions" with many possible answers are enough:

| What identifies you | Out of | Identified |
|---|---|---|
| 4 phone location pings (which tower, which hour) | 1.5 million people | 95% |
| 4 credit-card purchases (which shop, which day) | 1.1 million people | 90% |
| about 8 movie ratings, with approximate dates | Netflix subscribers | 99% |
: {tbl-colwidths="[58,27,15]"}

::: notes
Only 22 of the 100 are alone on their card; the class uses 54 of the 64
possible cards, and the biggest group shares one card four ways.
Guaranteed: 100 students, 64 cards, so at least two share a card -- in fact at
most 64 can be alone, so at least 36 share (the pigeonhole principle; capacity
from lecture 17). We come back to this dataset for the pigeonhole principle.
Sources: de Montjoye et al., "Unique in the Crowd", Scientific Reports 2013
(phone); de Montjoye et al., "Unique in the shopping mall", Science 2015
(credit cards); Narayanan & Shmatikov 2008 (Netflix Prize). The classic is
Sweeney (ZIP, birth date, sex) -- left off the slide on purpose. The
data-science response: k-anonymity -- release data only if every row shares
its profile with at least k - 1 others. Our class is not even 2-anonymous
(22 students are unique).
Why 4 pings beat 6 questions: a ping isn't yes/no -- it is one of thousands
of towers times thousands of hours, millions of possible answers. Four of them
give vastly more possible cards than people; we have 64 cards (6 bits) for
100 people. Fraction alone ~ e^(-n/m): e^(-100/64) ~ 21 students (actual 22).
Finding the twins efficiently is next week's tutorial... (set
aside for now).
:::

# Counting a Union

## Inclusion-Exclusion

Experiment using the code below, and then complete the observation:

For any sets $A$ and $B$: $|A\cup B| = \boxed{\phantom{|A| + |B| - |A \cap B|}}$

```{pyodide}
#| echo: false
#| output: false
import pandas as pd
df = pd.read_csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/UBC-CS/dsci220/refs/heads/main/data/imaginary_class.csv")
C, M, P, I = df['coffee'], df['morning'], df['pet'], df['instrument']
```

```{pyodide}
lhs = (C | M).sum()
guess = C.sum() + M.sum()
print(lhs, guess)
```

::: notes
Start from Monday's table: |C| + |M| = 56 + 45 = 101, but |C u M| = 70. The 31
students in C n M were counted twice -- once in C, once in M -- so subtract
them once: 56 + 45 - 31 = 70.
A hidden cell on this slide loads the imaginary class and defines C, M, P
(pet) and I (instrument) as masks. Later cells use those names, so they keep
working even after the cafe cell replaces df.
:::

## Check Your Regions {.activity .smaller}

Each region is a mask. Write one for each region and compare with your diagram.

```{pyodide}
print("C and M, not P:", (C & M & ~P).sum())
# your turn: the other seven regions

print("in C or M or P:", (C | M | P).sum())
```

For any sets $A$, $B$, $C$: $|A\cup B\cup C| = \boxed{\phantom{|A|+|B|+|C| - |A\cap B| - |A\cap C| - |B\cap C| + |A\cap B\cap C|}}$

::: notes
Answers: C&~M&~P 12, ~C&M&~P 7, ~C&~M&P 17, C&M&~P 15, C&~M&P 13, ~C&M&P 7,
C&M&P 16, ~C&~M&~P 13. The blank: |A|+|B|+|C| - |AnB| - |AnC| - |BnC| + |AnBnC|.
:::

# The Empty Set, Subsets, and Power Sets

## The Empty Set ($\varnothing$) {.smaller}

**Definition:** $\varnothing$ (a.k.a. $\{\}$) is the **unique set with no elements**.

- **Cardinality:** $|\varnothing|=0$.
- **Universal subset fact:** For any set $A$, $\varnothing\subseteq A$.
- **But membership is different:** $\varnothing\in A$ only if $A$ literally contains the empty set as an element.

**Examples**

- If $S=\{a,b\}$:  $\varnothing\subseteq S$, but NOT $\varnothing\in S$.  
- If $T=\{\varnothing,\{a\}\}$:  $\varnothing\in T$.



## Operations with $\varnothing$  {.smaller}

For any set $A$:

- **Union:** $A\cup\varnothing = A$
- **Intersection:** $A\cap\varnothing = \varnothing$
- **Difference:** $A - \varnothing = A$,  $\ \varnothing\setminus A = \varnothing$
- **Complement (in $U$):** $U - \varnothing = U$
- **Cardinalities:** $|A\cup\varnothing|=|A|$, $|A\cap\varnothing|=0$

::: notes
Quick demo with a tiny set on the board or in code; emphasize “subset vs element.”
:::


## Selecting Nobody {.activity .smaller}

Both of these masks select **nobody**. Run them.

```{pyodide}
print(( C & ~C ).sum())
print(( M & ~C & I ).sum())
```

Which one would select nobody in **any** class? Which one is empty only in **this** class?

::: notes
C & ~C is a contradiction: false in every row of its truth table (lectures
5-6), so it is empty for every dataset. M & ~C & I (morning, no coffee, plays
an instrument) is empty only because no student in this class fits -- add one
such student and it isn't. Both are the empty set here; only one is empty by
logic. This is the "nobody" question from the old Design a Set slide, which
Monday's deck didn't reach.
:::

## Element vs Subset

- $x\in S$ means **$x$ is one item** in $S$.
- $A\subseteq S$ means **every element of $A$** is in $S$.

**Examples (watch the braces!)**

- If $S=\{a,b\}$ then:
  - $a\in S$ is **true**; $\{a\}\in S$ is **false**; $\{a\}\subseteq S$ is **true**.
  - $\emptyset \in S$ is **false**; $\emptyset \subseteq S$ is **true**.
- If $T=\{\emptyset,\{a\}\}$ then:
  - $\emptyset \in T$ is **true**; $\{\emptyset\}\subseteq T$ is **true**.

::: notes
Say aloud: “Curly braces change the *type* of thing. Elements vs sets of elements.”
:::

## Quick Checks 

Let $S=\{\texttt{tea},\texttt{coffee},\texttt{juice}\}$.

1. $\texttt{tea}\in S$  ____  
2. $\{\texttt{tea}\}\in S$  ____  
3. $\{\texttt{tea}\}\subseteq S$  ____  
4. $\emptyset \subseteq S$  ____  
5. $\{\texttt{water}\}\subseteq S$  ____

::: notes
Answers: 1✓, 2✗, 3✓, 4✓, 5✗.
:::


## Power Set 

**Definition:** $\mathcal{P}(S)$ = the set of **all subsets** of $S$.

\

Example: 

If $S=\{a,b\}$,
$\ \mathcal{P}(S)=$ \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_

\ 

**Cardinality:** 

If $|S|=n$, then $|\mathcal{P}(S)|=$ \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_

## Why $2^n$? 

**Bitstring encoding:**  
Consider $S=\{s_1,\dots,s_n\}$. For each subset $T\subseteq S$ define an indicator of membership:
$$(b_1,\dots,b_n)\ \text{where } b_i=\begin{cases}1,& s_i\in T\\ 0,& s_i\notin T\end{cases}.$$

How many subsets of a set of size $n$?

::: notes
Connect to yesterday’s “$b$ bits $\Rightarrow 2^b$ codes.” Subsets $\leftrightarrow$ $n$-bit strings.
The ID cards are the example: each card is the set of questions that person
answered yes to, a subset of the six questions. So the 64 possible cards are
exactly P(six questions), and the card's 6-bit # is its bitstring.
:::

## Quick Check: 

Let $S=\{A,B,C\}$.

- Bitstring $101$ corresponds to subset $\{\_\_\_\_\}$.
- Subset $\{B\}$ corresponds to bitstring $\_\_\_\_\_\_$.


## Empty Sets and Power Sets


- $\varnothing\in \mathcal{P}(A)$ (since $\varnothing\subseteq A$)  
- $\mathcal{P}(\varnothing)=\{\varnothing\}$ and $|\mathcal{P}(\varnothing)|=1$



## Exit Ticket

What does knowing which sets someone belongs to tell you about them?

# If Time

## Cartesian Product $A\times B$ 

**Definition:** $A\times B=\{(a,b)\mid a\in A,\ b\in B\}$ 

**Cardinality:** $|A\times B|=|A|\cdot|B|$.

**Example:** $A=\{\texttt{iced},\texttt{hot}\}$, $B=\{\texttt{Latte},\texttt{Tea},\texttt{Mocha}\}$.

\ 

Then
$$A\times B=
\{(\texttt{iced},\texttt{Latte}),(\texttt{iced},\texttt{Tea}),(\texttt{iced},\texttt{Mocha}),$$
$$(\texttt{hot},\texttt{Latte}),(\texttt{hot},\texttt{Tea}),(\texttt{hot},\texttt{Mocha})\},$$

and $|A\times B|=2\cdot 3=6$.


## Code

```{pyodide}

import itertools
A = ['iced','hot']
B = ['Latte','Tea','Mocha']
list(itertools.product(A,B))

```

# From the 2025 deck

## From subsets to dataframe masks 

A Boolean **mask** over rows is an indicator vector $\in\{0,1\}^{|U|}$.

- Choosing rows is the same as selecting a **subset** of the universe $U$.
- $|$mask$|$ (sum of Trues) = cardinality of that subset.

## Union Example {.smaller}

Let  
$A=\{x\mid x.\mathrm{is\_iced}\}$ and  
$B=\{x\mid x.\mathrm{milk}\in\{\text{Oat, Almond}\}\}$.

- **Math:** $A\cup B$  
- **Predicate:** $\{\,x\in U \mid x.\mathrm{is\_iced}\ \lor\ x.\mathrm{milk}\in\{\text{Oat, Almond}\}\,\}$  
- **Mask:** `(df['is_iced']) | (df['milk'].str.strip().isin(['Oat','Almond']))`

## Design a Set {.activity .smaller}

Using only the six questions, write a mask that selects:

1. **exactly** the person on your card;
2. exactly your person **and** your neighbour's;
3. **nobody** at all.

```{pyodide}
me = df['coffee'] & ~df['morning']      # keep going...
df[me]['name'].tolist()
```

::: notes
1. An AND of all six answers (or fewer, if fewer already pin them down). Some
   can't be isolated: 78 of the 100 share their card with someone (Amara & Ravi,
   Leila & Hana, and many more).
2. Usually no single AND works -- you need an OR of two ANDs (each person's
   exact description). Any group can be written this way: an OR of ANDs, the
   DNF counterpart of lectures 6-7's CNF.
3. Two kinds of nobody: coffee & ~coffee is empty by logic (a contradiction);
   morning & ~coffee & instrument is empty only in THIS data. Run it.
:::
